stem: A bag contains 7 red marbles, 4 blue marbles, and 3 green marbles. If one marble is selected at random, what is the probability that the marble is blue?

options.text: \dfrac{1}{7}
\dfrac{2}{7}

explanation: The total number of marbles is 7 + 4 + 3 = 14. The probability of selecting a blue marble is 4/14, which simplifies to 2/7. The value 1/7 results from incorrectly simplifying 4/14 as if it were 2/14. The value 3/14 comes from using the count of green marbles instead of blue marbles. The value 4/11 results from dividing the blue count by only the non-blue marbles (7 + 3 = 10, misread as 11) instead of the total.

stem: A survey of 200 employees found that 78 drink coffee, 53 drink tea, and 19 drink both coffee and tea. If an employee is chosen at random, what is the probability that the employee drinks coffee or tea?

options.text: \dfrac{3}{4}

explanation: Using the inclusion-exclusion principle, the number who drink coffee or tea is 78 + 53 - 19 = 112. The probability is 112/200, which simplifies to 14/25. The value 131/200 results from adding 78 + 53 without subtracting the 19 who drink both. The value 19/200 represents only those who drink both, not those who drink either. The value 3/4 (150/200) comes from an incorrect setup that overestimates the union.

stem: A class has 31 students. Of these, 13 are in the debate club, 11 are in the science club, and 5 are in both clubs. If a student who is in the debate club is selected at random, what is the probability that this student is NOT in the science club?
explanation: Given that the student is in the debate club, the sample space is the 13 debate club members. Of these 13, exactly 5 are also in the science club, so 13 - 5 = 8 are in the debate club only. The conditional probability is 8/13. The value 5/13 results from finding the probability of being in the science club given debate club membership rather than not being in it. The value 8/31 incorrectly uses the total class size as the denominator instead of conditioning on debate club membership. The value 18/31 uses the total class size and miscounts students not in the science club.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A random sample of 250 voters in a city found that 145 support a new park proposal. Based on this sample, what is the best estimate of the percentage of all voters in the city who support the proposal?
explanation: The sample proportion is 145/250 = 0.58, or 58%. This is the best point estimate of the population proportion. The value 42% is the complement (100% - 58%), representing those who do not support the proposal. The value 52% comes from an arithmetic error in the division. The value 68% results from an incorrect calculation such as misreading the sample size.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A poll of 400 randomly selected residents found that 54% preferred candidate X, with a margin of error of 3.5 percentage points. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this result?

options.text: Exactly 54% of all residents prefer candidate X.
Between 50.5% and 57.5% of all residents are plausibly estimated to prefer candidate X.
If the poll were repeated, exactly 54% of respondents would prefer candidate X every time.
At most 57.5% of all residents prefer candidate X.

explanation: A margin of error of 3.5 percentage points means the plausible range for the true population proportion is 54% plus or minus 3.5%, which gives the interval from 50.5% to 57.5%. Stating that exactly 54% of all residents prefer candidate X treats the sample statistic as the exact population parameter, ignoring sampling variability. Claiming the result would be exactly 54% every time misunderstands that sample results vary across different samples. Saying at most 57.5% captures only the upper bound and omits the lower bound of the interval.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A researcher surveys a random sample of 600 high school students and finds that 37% participate in after-school athletics. The margin of error for this estimate is 4 percentage points at a 95% confidence level. A second researcher surveys a random sample of 150 students from the same population. If the second sample yields the same proportion, how will the margin of error for the second sample compare to that of the first?

options.text: It will be approximately the same because the sample proportion is the same.
It will be smaller because smaller samples produce more precise estimates.
It will be approximately 8 percentage points because the margin of error is inversely proportional to the sample size.
It will be approximately 8 percentage points because the margin of error is inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size.

explanation: The margin of error is inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size. With the sample size reduced from 600 to 150, the ratio of sample sizes is 600/150 = 4, so the square root of this ratio is 2. The margin of error for the second sample is approximately 4 times 2 = 8 percentage points. Claiming the margin stays the same ignores the effect of sample size on precision. Saying smaller samples are more precise reverses the actual relationship. Stating the margin of error is inversely proportional to the sample size (rather than its square root) applies the wrong relationship and would yield 16 percentage points.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A school counselor reviews student records and finds that students who participate in at least one extracurricular activity have higher grade point averages than students who do not participate in any. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.text: Participating in extracurricular activities causes higher grades.
There is an association between participation in extracurricular activities and higher grade point averages.
Students should be required to join an extracurricular activity to improve their grades.
Students with higher grades have more free time for extracurricular activities.

explanation: Because this is an observational study based on reviewing existing records without random assignment, only an association can be established, not causation. Claiming that participation causes higher grades asserts causation, which requires a randomized controlled experiment. Recommending that students be required to join activities goes beyond what the data supports and introduces a policy judgment. Stating that students with higher grades have more free time reverses the direction and asserts a causal claim without evidence.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: Researchers randomly assign 120 participants to two groups. One group receives a new herbal supplement daily for 8 weeks, while the other group receives an identical-looking placebo. Neither the participants nor the researchers measuring outcomes know which group each participant is in. At the end of the study, the supplement group shows significantly lower stress levels. Which feature of the study design allows the researchers to conclude that the supplement likely caused the reduction in stress?

options.text: The use of a placebo that looks identical to the supplement
The random assignment of participants to the two groups
The fact that neither participants nor researchers knew the group assignments
The 8-week duration of the study

explanation: Random assignment is the key feature that allows a causal conclusion, because it ensures that confounding variables are approximately equally distributed across the treatment and control groups. The identical placebo controls for the placebo effect but does not itself establish causation. Double-blinding (neither participants nor researchers knowing assignments) reduces bias in measurement and behavior but is not the feature that establishes causal inference. The 8-week duration affects the study's ability to detect effects but does not enable causal conclusions.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A university researcher wants to determine whether a new study technique improves exam scores. She recruits 90 volunteers and lets each choose whether to use the new technique or their usual method. Students who choose the new technique score an average of 7 points higher. A campus newspaper reports that the new technique boosts exam scores by 7 points. Which of the following best explains why the newspaper's claim may not be valid?

options.text: The sample size of 90 is too small to detect a 7-point difference.
Students who chose the new technique may differ systematically from those who did not, making it impossible to attribute the difference solely to the technique.
The study did not use a placebo, so the results are unreliable.
The 7-point difference is not statistically significant because no confidence interval was reported.

explanation: Because participants self-selected into groups rather than being randomly assigned, there may be confounding variables. Students who chose the new technique may be more motivated, better organized, or otherwise systematically different from those who did not. This self-selection bias means the 7-point difference cannot be attributed solely to the technique. A sample of 90 is not inherently too small to detect such a difference. The absence of a placebo is a concern in some experiments but is not the fundamental flaw here; the lack of random assignment is. Whether a confidence interval was reported is a reporting concern, not the core design flaw that undermines the causal claim.
